title: How I program my Deadlift days for Natural Hypertrophy
summary: His two deadlift days. Day 1 is heavy conventional pulls (raw, strapped), speed triples, heavy rows supersetted with stiff-leg deadlifts, then trap, lat, calf and hyperextension work. Day 2 is snatch-grip deadlifts, deadlift-stance SSB box squats, Yates rows and rack pulls. He pulls conventional only once per cycle because frequent conventional deadlifting makes him plateau, and he aims the accessories at his weak points (lats, traps, hamstrings).

claims.claim: He has never had recovery issues or injuries from deadlifting and can pull frequently, but deadlifting too often always led him to plateau.
His goal is to gain deadlift strength without burning his CNS, because heavy deadlifting makes him more injury-prone on squats, where he usually hurts his back.
He pulls conventional and hates sumo; he tried sumo for about 8 months last year and reached roughly 335 lbs for sets of 8.
With his vertical torso and already overpowered glutes, sumo only made him feel his glutes, not his back, traps or legs, so it made a strong point even more dominant.
Deadlift day 1 opens with conventional deadlifts for 1-3 heavy sets of 2-5 reps, raw without a belt (he doesn't like belts) and with straps.
Every bodybuilder should use lifting straps; pulling without straps makes no sense to him.
He then does speed deadlifts for 4 sets of triples and only adds weight when all sets fly up fast.
He supersets speed deadlifts with leg raises and band work for shoulder mobility and thoracic extension; strong thoracic extension is in his view the most important thing for staying healthy.
He supersets heavy barbell rows with stiff-leg deadlifts but advises others not to: both need flexible, strong hamstrings and a very strong, stable lower back, otherwise it is a recipe for injury.
He adds towel-grip work to the row/stiff-leg superset for 4 sets, then snatch-grip shrugs, wide-grip pull-ups and leg raises.
His training targets his weak points: his 'deadlift day' is really a hamstrings, lower back, glutes and upper back day with emphasis on specific upper back muscles.
Heavy rows tax his lats, snatch-grip shrugs target his traps (not big enough), and wide-grip pull-ups again hit the lats because he wants big lats.
He trains calves (piano and Toshiki raises) on 3 of every 4 lower body days and hyperextensions on 3 of 4, overlapping on both deadlift days.
Deadlift day 1 ends with wide-grip pull-ups, hyperextensions, grippers for forearms and ab training.
He avoids pulling conventional from the floor too often because he stagnates; on day 2 he uses snatch-grip deadlifts for higher reps (4-8) since they feel natural to him.
The deadlift-stance safety squat bar box squat is in his view the best accessory for raising the conventional deadlift, maybe better than deadlift variations; it targets glutes and hamstrings.
Day 2 continues with towel grip, Yates rows from the rack (partial), wide-grip pull-ups and rack pulls for lats and traps, then calves and hyperextensions.
Snatch-grip deadlifts emphasize the lower back and quads, so the SSB box squat covers glutes and hamstrings and the rows and rack pulls cover traps and lats.
He deadlifts every 4 days, two days after his squat session; because everything is planned, he recovers and grows despite high lower body frequency.
He prioritizes the long-term risk-to-reward of pulling over pulling every day.
